name: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
title: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
answer: Drafting statements and disclosures covers the preparation of the narrative and numerical text that accompanies financial results, including management commentary, notes to the accounts, risk factors, and regulatory filings. In an AI context the work spans two directions: using language models to produce or redraft disclosure text, and disclosing the use of AI systems themselves where they affect reported figures or controls. The scope reaches anyone who signs off on a filing, not only the analyst who writes the first draft. It sits alongside the numbers rather than replacing them, because a statement is only as good as the ledger it describes.

sections.body: Drafting statements and disclosures covers the preparation of the narrative and numerical text that accompanies financial results, including management commentary, notes to the accounts, risk factors, and regulatory filings. In an AI context the work spans two directions: using language models to produce or redraft disclosure text, and disclosing the use of AI systems themselves where they affect reported figures or controls. The scope reaches anyone who signs off on a filing, not only the analyst who writes the first draft. It sits alongside the numbers rather than replacing them, because a statement is only as good as the ledger it describes.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a document pipeline rather than a single model. Source material arrives from the general ledger, consolidation systems, prior-year filings, and internal policy documents, then passes through retrieval and drafting tools that keep the model grounded in approved text. Version control and an audit trail matter as much as the model choice, since a disclosure can be revised many times before it is filed. Most teams keep a human editor in the loop and treat model output as a draft, not a finished statement.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical cycle starts with a template drawn from the previous period, then fills each section from current data and approved language. The model is asked to summarise movements, flag inconsistencies between narrative and figures, and suggest wording that matches the house style. Reviewers check every number against the underlying schedules and every claim against evidence, because a fluent sentence can still be wrong. The final text is locked, signed, and archived with the prompts and sources that produced it.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Responsibility for a filed statement stays with the preparer and the signatory, whatever tool produced the draft. Firms therefore keep records of which model version was used, what data it saw, and who edited the output, so the provenance of each sentence can be reconstructed. Disclosure rules on forward-looking statements, materiality, and insider information apply to AI-assisted text exactly as they apply to text written by hand.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter coupling between the reporting system and the drafting layer, so that a change in the numbers propagates into the narrative automatically. Regulators are moving toward explicit questions about AI use in reporting, which will push firms to document their tooling more formally. Smaller teams will likely gain access to drafting help that was previously affordable only to large issuers. The open question is not whether models can write a disclosure, but whether the review process around them can keep pace.
